articles.title: Purdue Football: Depth Chart Review – Offense – Illinois
articles.summary: Purdue’s offense wasn’t perfect, but a couple of big plays in the passing game helped seal a routine Big 10 road victory over Illinois.
articles.body:
It finally happened: Purdue ended up on the correct side of a Big 10 ledger for the first time since the 2024 Indiana victory. I want to remind everyone that I predicted this outcome…just don't look at the other outcomes I may have gotten slightly incorrect along the way.

While I predicted a Purdue victory, I was wrong about the method of delivery. I thought it was going to take a Herculean effort from the offense, but somehow, the defense ended up as the star of the show. Ryan Browne, Fame Ijeboi, and company were OK, but I thought they were better against both Wake and UCLA. Luckily, the defense wasn't facing the Illinois offense, not the Demon Deacon or Bruin offense.

In the end, the offense made enough plays to win the game. The wide receivers made a couple of big plays; Ryan Browne didn't throw the ball to the wrong team; the run game did enough to keep the Illinois defense honest. Short-yardage and goal-to-go situations remained a struggle, but Antonio Harris gives me hope it won't be as big of a problem moving forward.

For the first time in forever, the program feels like it's trending in the right direction.

Ryan Browne : Snaps – 61 – Comp – 18/27 (69.7) – Yds – 255 – Td – 1 – Int – 0 – Rushes – 5 – Yds – -2

That was a good performance from Browne, good, but not great. I docked him half a grade for Purdue's continued struggle to cash in touchdowns inside the 10-yard line. Obviously, that's not all on Browne, but I need to put the blame somewhere. Heavy is the head that wears the quarterback crown, and whatnot.

He piloted one of the most important 4th-quarter drives in recent Purdue history when the offense received the ball after an Illinois field goal, up 6, with 8 minutes remaining. After a weirdly important kickoff return by reserve tight end Hayden Timosciek gave the Boilermakers solid field position at their 40, Browne completed 3 out of 4 passes, including a highlight real 31-yard pass to Chauncey Magwood, which put the ball on the 1-foot line. Not going to lie, Magwood not getting into the end zone felt like a bad omen, but Antonio Harris pushed the ball over the goal line on 2nd down to put Purdue up by 2 touchdowns with 4:30 remaining.

At this point, I think it's safe to say that Browne is in the upper quadrant of Big 10 signal callers. Not too shabby for a guy who was predicted to be the worst quarterback in the Big 10 coming into the season. Browne's improvement, aided by the massive influx of talent on offense, has the Boilermakers, for now, out of the Big 10 basement and playing with confidence.

Fame Ijeboi : Snaps – 49 – Rushes – 19 – Yds – 65 (3.4 YPC) – Tds – 0 – Rec – 1 – Yds – 10

Antonio Harris: Snaps – 18 – Rushes – 6 – Yds – 20 (3.3 YPC) – Tds – 1 – Rec – 1 – Yds – 4

Jerrick Gibson: Snaps – 4 – Rushes – 1 – Yds – 5 (5 YPC) – Tds – 0 – Rec – 1 – Yds – 9

That wasn't Fame's best performance. He struggled to find anything in Purdue's interior run game, and his attempt to bounce off a tackle inside the 5-yard line cost Purdue a second-and-third-down run attempt to put the ball in the end zone; the offense settled for a field goal instead of a touchdown. I liked the effort, but the situational awareness was lacking. He ended up with 2 rushes for over 10 yards, with a long of 14. His best play came in the passing game when he turned a well-covered swing pass on 3rd and 9 into a 1st and 10 on determination alone in the 3rd quarter. That drive ended in a field goal and kept Purdue's defense off the field for much of the 3rd quarter.

It appears Antonio Harris has carved out a role in the offense as the short yardage back. Purdue needed a solution to their short-yardage woes, and the 6'1", 215-pound junior running back provided one on Saturday. He picked up 2 short-yardage first downs and punched in a touchdown on the goal line.

Jerrick Gibson has been oddly efficient in his brief cameos. It feels like he shows up, has a respectable run, and then disappears for the rest of the game. Depth is crucial at running back. I like that the coaching staff is trying to keep Gibson involved, even if it's just a carry or two a game.

Chauncey Magwood : Snaps – 58 – Targets – 6 – Rec – 4 – Yds – 53

Xavier Townsend: Snaps – 39 – Targets – 6 – Rec – 4 – Yds – 24

De'Nylon Morrissette : Snaps – 31 – Targets – 2 – Rec – 0

Assad Waseem: Snaps – 31 – Targets – 4 – Rec – 3 – Yds – 98

Tra'Mar Harris: Snaps – 19 – Targets – 3 – Rec – 3 – Yds – 52 – Tds – 1

Wasseem received his first start of the season and continued to establish himself as Purdue's top receiver. Only had 3 receptions, but one went for 61 yards, and another went for 24 yards. My only minor gripe with Waseem was that I didn't think he finished the 61-yard reception hard enough. He sort of petered out inside the 10 and was escorted out of bounds by the closing Illinois defensive backs. Listen man, I know you ran a long way, but the end zone was right in front of you, and your team hasn't exactly excelled inside the 10-yard line this season. You've got to try to get the ball in the end zone by any means necessary. Purdue's best bet for scoring touchdowns is to skip the redzone altogether.

I was wondering when someone would start chiseling into Morrissette's snaps, and it looks like Tra'Mar Harris began the process on Saturday. He gives Ryan Browne a big body at wideout who excels at corralling back-shoulder throws. He made his 21-yard touchdown reception look easy and allowed the Boilermaker offense to avoid the dreaded zone of touchdown death inside the 10.

It was shaping up to be a relatively uneventful day for Chauncey Magwood, and then he made one of the best receptions I've seen from a Purdue receiver since David Bell was hauling in circus catches on the regular. Next time, I humbly request he find a way to finish the play in the end zone and not on the 1, but Antonio Harris managed to cash in Magwood's amazing catch for 6 points, 2 plays later.

Morrissette was on the field on running downs more than on passing downs and once failed to make a catch. It seems like Browne is always looking for Morrissette in the red zone, but he can never find him. Xavier Townsend was active in the game plan but couldn't turn any of his short receptions into anything other than short receptions.

In terms of yardage, this wasn't the receiving group's best day, but Wasseem, Magwood, and Tra'Mar Harris all made crucial downfield catches that helped Purdue build a lead and play from ahead instead of chasing points. Explosive passing plays were key in securing the victory.

George Burhenn: Snaps – 26 – Targets – 1 – Rec – 1 – Yds – 8

After not playing against Notre Dame, George Burhenn returned to action and pulled down his lone target of the day; the other tight ends mainly function as additional blockers in short-yardage situations. Reserve center Ethan Trent also got a couple of goal-line snaps at tight end.

It was nice to see George back; this group did their job as far as I can tell. I'm going to make this grade a pass/fail, with the tight ends passing.

Purdue made two changes to the offensive line after the Notre Dame debacle. Marques Easley appears to have taken over left guard from Brock Brownfield, and freshman Rico Schrieber started for the first time in his short career for the injured Jude McCoskey.

After allowing 2 sacks, 3 quarterback hits, and 17 hurries against Notre Dame last week, the offensive line fared much better against an Illinois team that plays a similar game. Browne didn't take a sack, or even a hit, for that matter, on Saturday, and was only "hurried" 5 times. PFF attributed 2 of those 5 hurries to tight end Jackson Berryman. When they're not playing a team like Notre Dame, this group is better at pass protection than run blocking, and that played out on Saturday. Aside from the slightly undersized Micah Banuelos at right guard, who also happens to be the best run blocker of the bunch, this is a tall group of linemen who don't get much movement in the run game. When Purdue tried to lean on their run game late to salt the game away, Illinois forced multiple 3-and-outs. The next step in the maturation of this offensive line is to get a little lower with their pads and a little nastier in their attitude when it's time to run the ball.

Penalties were an issue with this group. They were hit with 7 penalties (1 declined), including yet another false start inside the 10-yard line.

They're not going to steamroll anyone in the run game, but if they can keep giving Ryan Browne time to throw, as they did on Saturday, it's a unit that's trending in the right direction. Keep in mind, Easley and Banuelos hadn't started a game until this season, and Rico Schrieber was playing high school ball last year. On top of that, Nuku Mafi was brought in to play guard, but is filling in admirably for Joey Tanona at left tackle. He might be the most important portal pickup for what is shaping up to be a great 2025 crop of transfers for Barry Odom.

This is a tough grade. Considering the penalties and continued short-yardage issues, this was probably a C performance, but considering the youth of this group, I'm not sure how much more you can ask from them…so I'm going with a B.

articles.title: Peru ground game outpaces Moriah
articles.summary: MINEVILLE — Peru senior Brody Blaise- Smith led the charge, complemented by Ausable Valley’s Deon Lawyer, as the Nighthawks’ running game proved too much for...
articles.body:
MINEVILLE — Peru senior Brody Blaise- Smith led the charge, complemented by Ausable Valley's Deon Lawyer, as the Nighthawks' running game proved too much for the Moriah Vikings Friday night at Linney Field.

Blaise-Smith ran for 151 yards and two touchdowns, while Lawyer racked up 75 yards in Peru's 28-6 win in Mineville. Logan Porter also ran for 41 yards and a touchdown on just three carries.

It was a dramatic change from the previous week's win over Saranac Lake, in which the Nighthawks relied on the arm of quarterback Drew Engstrom for four touchdowns and the running game was held to 130 yards and no points before an 82-yard David Nwadike run in the dying seconds.

"Our rush game was working amazingly today," Engstrom said. "Our pass game was a little off in the first half. I was missing easy throws. [Moriah] came out in something that we've never seen before, so it was a little different, and we got used to it in the second half."

Head coach Ryon O'Connell was happy with how his team adapted.

"Yes, it wasn't as explosive as weeks past, but I'm fine with that," O'Connell said. "If you're going to be a good football team, you have to find ways to win in different ways."

The Nighthawks didn't just control the ground game on offense. Their defense held the Vikings' Skyler Frasier-led run game to just 2.5 yards per carry.

While the story of the game largely played out on the ground, the first points on the board actually came through the air, as Engstrom completed a pass to Isaiah Hendrix, who beat a couple tacklers and dove into a full stretch to get to the goal line.

"We realized that they were playing 10 yards off the ball and not looking at me, so we could get him on a quick curl," Engstrom said. "Isaiah is a hard guy to tackle, so we knew that he had a great matchup against that kid, and we trusted him."

Blaise-Smith doubled the lead midway through the second quarter. In a 4th&11 play on the 35 yard line, the Nighthawks went with a draw play that set Blaise-Smith free up the middle all the way to the end zone.

"We knew that they thought we were going to pass, so we spread them out," Engstrom said. "Then, we knew we could run it down their throat, so we did."

On the ensuing drive, Moriah mixed things up with some snaps directly to Frasier and, after a 10-play drive, found the end zone.

"Give credit to Moriah, that was a great drive," O'Connell said. "They came out in a formation we weren't ready for, and they did a great job driving the ball"

With just 36 seconds remaining before halftime, it seemed likely that would be the final score of the half, but the Nighthawks had other ideas.

Four plays and 28 seconds later, Peru responded with a touchdown of their own.

"We practice two-minutes, we practice one-minute drills, we practice one-time-out drills," O'Connell said. "The kids were calm, they were collected, and that was a big drive to get points."

The drive was capped off by another Blaise-Smith touchdown, this time from 31 yards out.

"The blocking was perfect," Blaise-Smith said. "I went untouched on both [touchdowns], so that's all on my linemen."

In the second half, Lawyer largely took over the running duties, coupled with some big chunk plays by Porter.

On Peru's last full drive of the game, they handed the ball to Lawyer on six straight plays, and he got within a yard of the goal line before fumbling it. Despite Lawyer not scoring, Blaise-Smith praised the way Lawyer contributed to the win.

"He played great," Blaise-Smith said. "It's awesome to be able to have a two-back approach like that, where they don't know what to expect with either of us. He's a really good addition to our team."

With the win, the Nighthawks improve to 5-0, 4-0 in the CVAC, and will prepare for a fierce rivalry game this weekend. Friday, Peru will host Beekmantown, who had a bye week this week but will be looking to carry some momentum from a win over Plattsburgh School the weekend before.

The game will kick off at 7 p.m. Friday in Peru.

articles.title: Arizona Cardinals' Week 4 offensive snap counts, observations vs. Giants
articles.summary: The Cardinals played 66 offensive snaps on Sunday against the Giants. See how the playing time was split up.
articles.body:
In the Arizona Cardinals ' 36-24 loss to the New York Giants , 17 players participated in at least one of the 66 offensive snaps.

Right guard Isaiah Adams suffered an ankle injury in the second quarter and played only 28 snaps. Jon Gaines II replaced him. Left tackle Paris Johnson Jr. missed the final snap of the game because of a torn biceps and was replaced by Jayden Williams.

Wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. was not on the field for 23 snaps during the game. Running back Tyler Allgeier played more snaps than Jeremiyah Love, who had trainers working on his ankle during the game. Love acknowledged it was about managing him after missing close to a month of practice because of a high-ankle sprain suffered on Aug. 13.

How was the playing time divided up? We have the numbers below.

The first number after each name is the snap count, and the second is the percentage. Players in bold were starters.

Protection issues continue to bedevil the passing game, forcing Brissett to often throw quickly, especially on the fateful four plays from the 4-yard line at the end of the game. Success in the close red zone often comes when the quarterback has time to find a receiver coming open. Overall, Brissett's 21 completions on 35 attempts averaged 7.9 yards and an abysmal 4.74 per attempt.

Three interceptions plummeted his passer rating in the game to 55.2 with two of the picks coming on a tipped ball and when his arm was hit while throwing. He did run four times for 18 yards. If there was more time on the clock at the end of the game, the best strategy might have been to simply have him run up the middle a few times.

Tyler Allgeier (36/55), Jeremiyah Love (30/45)

Did not play: Bam Knight (played only on special teams)

Injured reserve: James Conner (eligible to return after Week 4), Trey Benson

It started off strong on the first two drives with Love gaining 43 yards on six rushes and Allgeier three for 38, including a 22-yard touchdown. Production sank for the remainder of the game after that with Love 8-20 and Allgeier 5-4 (13-24 total). There was little in the passing game with Allgeier 2-7 and Love 1-minus 8.

Allgeier was in the game instead of Love at the end of the game because he's better in production than Love and healthier.

"It's frustrating because I'm the type of guy who is willing to do whatever I can to help the team have success," Love said. "I want to be out there regardless how I am feeling, but my coaches care about me. They're not going to put you out there if you're not in a position to be yourself. It's frustrating for me personally, not even with the coaches. I'm really frustrated with myself because I just want to be good. I want to be 100 percent."

NextGen Stats had Allgeier with 10 snaps in the red zone and Love only two.

"It's been a long year for me," Love said. "Body sometimes is down, sometimes it's tired. It's managing those things. Coaches know that. This is probably going to be the longest year of my life, and I want to manage that workload. So today, making sure they are managing me. They are doing what they need to do to keep me up for the rest of the season."

Michael Wilson (62/94), Marvin Harrison Jr. (43/65), Kendrick Bourne (42/64) , Jalen Brooks (3/5)

Did not play: Devin Duvernay, Simi Fehoko (both played only on special teams)

Wilson led the team in targets with 13 after having 17 the week before. He caught seven for 95 yards. Harrison had one reception and a touchdown for 12 yards in four targets. He wasn't able to make a catch on the late pass that resulted in a questionable pass-interference penalty that moved the Cardinals from the 22-yard to the 4-yard line. Bourne was never targeted.

Trey McBride (64/97), Elijah Higgins (24/36), Hunter Long (20/30)

PUP reserve: Tip Reiman (eligible to practice after Week 2 and play after Week 4)

It was another lackluster day for McBride, who caught only seven of 12 targets for a mere 31 yards (4.4 average). In the last two games, he has 16 catches for 106 yards (6.6 average). In Week 2 against Seattle, he averaged 4.1 yards on eight receptions for 41 yards. Higgins had two receptions for 17, one for a 2-yard touchdown.

Did not play: G/C Hayden Conner (played only on special teams)

The Cardinals now must deal with the loss of Johnson for the remainder of the season. Seventh-round pick Williams will be his likely replacement. In addition, Adams suffered an ankle injury. Gaines played all of the snaps in Week 1 against the Chargers when Adams was inactive because of a knee injury suffered in practice during the week of preparation for the Aug. 22 preseason game against the Cowboys.
